h:
Pick up your phone.

Somewhere beneath the glass, beneath the apps and the alerts and the glow, a small engine is working. It holds your messages. It remembers your contacts. It keeps the history of your browser, the settings of your apps, the record of what you did and when. It does this quietly, thousands of times a day, and it almost never fails.

You have never heard its name.

It is called SQLite. It is a database, a storehouse where information is kept and retrieved, and by any honest count it is the most widely deployed database on earth. It sits inside nearly every smartphone, inside the major web browsers, inside the systems that run your computer, inside programs you have used for years without a second thought. It carries no logo. It has no advertising campaign and no billionaire founder on magazine covers. It sells nothing and asks for nothing. It simply holds.

In an industry built on noise, it is the rare thing made to be silent and to last. Like a foundation stone, it is noticed only by the men who laid it.

The man who laid this one is D. Richard Hipp. Around the turn of the millennium, while working on a project for the U.S. Navy, he needed a database that could stand on its own feet: no server to fail, no keeper to tend it, nothing standing between the program and its data. Nothing on the market did what he needed, so he built it himself. He wrote it largely alone, with one close collaborator, and between the two of them they wrote nearly every line.

Then he did something almost no one in his trade does. He gave it away.

He didn’t make it free with conditions, or free under a license dictating who may use it and how. He placed it in the public domain. Anyone may take it, build on it, sell products made with it, and owe him nothing. Asked why, he answered with the plainness of a man who meant it: he wrote it because it was useful to him, and he released it hoping it would be useful to others.

Open almost any piece of commercial software and the first words you meet are a warning. Copyright. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use prohibited. The foundations of the modern world are fenced in legal iron, every gate posted with a threat.

Open SQLite, and the first words are these:

“The author disclaims copyright to this source code. In place of a legal notice, here is a blessing:

May you do good and not evil.

May you find forgiveness for yourself and forgive others.

May you share freely, never taking more than you give.”

And Under the title “Code of Ethics,” the builders of the most widely deployed database on earth have set down the rule they pledged to live by. Its first line is the first commandment.

The first is Moses, speaking to Israel on the plains of Moab (Deuteronomy 6:5).

Christ Himself set it above every other when asked which commandment stood first of all: “And you shall love the Lord your God out of all your heart and out of all your soul and out of all your mind and out of all your strength” (Mark 12:30).

The tenth is His own summons, word for word from the Gospel: “If anyone desires to come after Me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow Me” (Matthew 16:24). The builder did not invent a creed. He took the oldest commands in the book and bound his work to them.

So consider what that means. Every phone in every pocket, in every hospital, courtroom, newsroom, and parliament on earth, runs on an engine whose builders pledged themselves to the words of Scripture. The skeptic scrolling past a sermon he would never read is carrying it. So is the believer who holds his phone at arm’s length, half-convinced it belongs to the enemy.

Almost no one has read that page. Nearly everyone has carried it.

An Almost Sacred Meaning

The rule did not begin as a manifesto. It began as a box on a form.

As SQLite spread, the companies that depended on it began sending its builders paperwork: supplier registration forms, compliance questionnaires, the slow bureaucracy that follows anything the world comes to rely on. Somewhere on those forms sat a line that had become standard across the industry: attach your Code of Conduct. By the late 2010s, nearly every serious software project had one. Most were stitched from the same few templates, the same approved language, the same reporting procedures, enforced by committee.

Hipp found them vapid. He wanted something with more weight than trendy, feel-good statements. So when the box needed filling, he reached past the templates, past the century, past the whole modern world, to a document written by a monk named Benedict. The fourth chapter of Benedict’s Rule lists what he called the instruments of good works: seventy-two short commands, most of them lifted straight from Scripture. The Great Commandment. The Decalogue. The Sermon on the Mount. Written in Italy around 530, it had ordered the lives of praying communities for fifteen hundred years.

In October 2018, the tech world found it.

At first, developers asked whether it was a joke, a sarcastic reply to clients who had nagged the project for a code.

The assumption said more about them than about Hipp. Silicon Valley has long told itself that it stands above religion, that faith is something the smart people “outgrew” somewhere between the printing press and the microchip.

In that world, a serious engineer quoting a sixth-century monk could only be performing irony. Nobody who builds the future believes that stuff.

It was not a joke. Hipp confirmed he was serious, and that his core developers had pledged to live by it. Then the outrage began in earnest.

The most widely deployed database on earth had an official conduct policy telling its builders to love the Lord God with their whole heart, to chastise the body, to fear the Day of Judgment, to be in dread of hell.

Pause on what exactly offended them.

It was not a hidden agenda. The page stated plainly that no one was required to follow the Rule, to know the Rule, or even to think it a good idea. Anyone could take the code and live however they pleased. The Rule bound only the builders, and it bound them in one direction. They called it a covenant, a one-way promise: we will treat you this way regardless of how you treat us.

A handful of men publicly pledged to love their enemies, to bless those who cursed them, and never to return evil for evil, and they asked nothing of anyone in return. The industry that had spent years demanding codes of conduct found that one intolerable.

Hipp’s answer is worth studying. He did not rage, and he did not fold. He renamed the document. The official page now explains why: its builders had learned that “Code of Conduct” carries “a very specific and almost sacred meaning” for some readers, a meaning their document did not match. So it became a Code of Ethics, and beside it he installed a pre-packaged, widely approved Code of Conduct to satisfy the critics. Then he said the quiet part plainly. The particular were satisfied, and “we old-school developers can keep our Benedictine Rule.”

He even cited his authority for the retreat: Rule 71. Make peace with your adversary before the sun sets.

He yielded the label. He kept the ground. The Rule still stands on the official site today, all seventy-two lines, Christ and Judgment and hell included, laid over the foundation of nearly every phone you have ever held.

Measure, Number, and Weight

Scripture smells of sawdust and hot bronze more often than we remember.

The first time God speaks of filling a man with His Spirit, the man is not a prophet, a priest, or a king. He is a craftsman. “I have filled him with a divine spirit of wisdom, and understanding, and knowledge,” the Lord says of Bezalel, “to invent in every work, and to frame works, to labour in gold, silver, brass, blue, purple, and spun scarlet, and works in stone, and for artificers’ work in wood, to work at all works” (Exodus 31:3-5).

The tabernacle, the dwelling place of God among His people, was raised by men whose hands had been anointed for the trade.

Go back further. When judgment came for the whole earth, the survival of the human kind rode on a work of engineering. God did not hand Noah a miracle. He handed him a specification: “Make therefore for thyself an ark of square timber; thou shalt make the ark in compartments, and thou shalt pitch it within and without with pitch. And thus shalt thou make the ark; three hundred cubits the length of the ark, and fifty cubits the breadth, and thirty cubits the height of it” (Genesis 6:14-15). Salvation came through a built thing, built exactly to measure.

Go forward. When Solomon raised the temple, he “sent, and took Chiram out of Tyre,” a craftsman the text describes as “a worker in brass, and accomplished in art and skill and knowledge to work every work in brass” (3 Kingdoms 7:1-2).

Bezalel raised the tabernacle. Chiram cast the pillars, the sea, and the lavers of the temple. Both times, the house of God was built by a craftsman’s hands. When Nehemiah rebuilt the broken walls of Jerusalem, half the workers “wrought the work, and half of them kept guard,” and “those who carried the burdens were under arms: each with one hand wrought his work, and with the other held his dart. And the builders wrought each man having his sword girt upon his loins, and so they built” (Nehemiah 4:16-18). They built, and they guarded what they built.

And when the Word through whom all things were made took on flesh, He spent most of His years on earth as a builder. The people of Nazareth said so themselves: “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary, and brother of James and Joses and Judas and Simon? And are not His sisters here with us?” And they were taking offense at Him (Mark 6:3).

The Greek word is tekton: a craftsman, a builder. The Septuagint uses that very word of Chiram, the temple’s worker in bronze. The hands that would be nailed to wood had spent decades shaping it.

Scripture does record building projects God opposed, and it is worth being precise about why. At Babel it fell on the purpose: a name for the builders, and one power no one could scatter. “Come, let us build to ourselves a city and tower, whose top shall be to heaven, and let us make to ourselves a name, before we are scattered abroad upon the face of all the earth” (Genesis 11:4).

The Book of Enoch, which the Ethiopian Church has kept in its canon, records the same pattern from the other side: “And Azazel taught men to make swords, and knives, and shields, and breastplates, and made known to them the metals of the earth and the art of working them, and bracelets, and ornaments, and the use of antimony, and the beautifying of the eyelids, and all kinds of costly stones, and all colouring tinctures. And there arose much godlessness, and they committed fornication, and they were led astray, and became corrupt in all their ways” (1 Enoch 8:1-2).

Kingdom Code has traced Azazel’s curriculum before. Read that record closely and the line runs exactly here. The Watchers did not invent bronze; the Spirit would later fill Bezalel to work it. They handed it down out of its order, to men not made ready, for ends that were not God’s. The sin in Enoch 8 is not the forge. It is who opened it, and why.

In neither case did God condemn the craft. He judged the name the builders built for, and the order they built outside of.

Neither judgment fell on the craft. It fell on the ambition behind it: a name for the builders, and knowledge pulled out of its order. The line in Scripture was never drawn between building and not building. It was drawn between building under God’s measure and building to seize what belongs to Him.

The Wisdom of Solomon, preserved in the old canons, gives that measure in a single sentence:

“Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight” - Wisdom 11:20

Creation is not chaos. It is order kept in its place: every star numbered, every kind fixed, nothing lost.

Consider what a database actually is. It is measure and number. Records kept in order, each in its place, retrieved exactly as they were set down, nothing lost. The most widely deployed one on earth was built by a man who made that order his trade, and then did the opposite of Babel.

The Only Question

Pick up your phone again.

Nothing about it has changed since you started reading. The glass is the same, the glow is the same, and the small engine beneath it is still keeping your messages in order, still holding your records in their place. What has changed is that you now know what is written at its foundation.

There is a kind of believer who looks at the world of screens and code and sees only enemy country: a territory already surrendered, to be endured, resisted, or fled. The instinct is not foolish. Babylon has always loved its machinery, and the Scriptures never ask us to be naive about what empires build or why. But the instinct carries an assumption it rarely examines: that the ground itself belongs to the enemy, and that the faithful keep themselves clean by staying off it.

Scripture’s faithful men never believed that.

Joseph ran the storehouses of Egypt, the greatest empire of his age. He kept its grain and kept its count, gathering so much that he stopped counting: “And Joseph gathered very much grain as the sand of the sea, until it could not be numbered, for there was no number of it.” - Genesis 41:49

He managed Pharaoh’s stores and never bowed to Pharaoh’s gods. Daniel served in the courts of Babylon itself, trained in the learning of the Chaldeans and found ten times better than all its wise men (Daniel 1:20). He administered the kingdom, and when the king’s decree demanded his worship, he opened his windows toward Jerusalem and prayed three times a day, as he always had (Daniel 6:10).

Neither man mistook the storehouse for the altar. They worked inside the machinery of empires and refused its worship. The line they held was never the tool. It was the knee.

That is what D. Richard Hipp understood. He did not flee the trade because the world runs on it. He did not bless the world’s assumptions to keep his clients comfortable. He built the thing better than anyone else could, gave it away, set Christ’s commands at its foundation, and when the industry demanded he take them down, he changed a label and left the Rule standing.

Ground that the faithful abandon does not stay holy. It is simply handed to someone else, and the someone else will write his own words at the foundation, and they will not be a blessing.

Someone was always going to lay the foundations. The only question was who.

Most Christians will grant that the faith laid the foundations of the civilized world: the hospital, the university, the rule of law, the dignity of the weak. But we speak of it the way men speak of ruins, as something our fathers built and we merely inherited. We treat the Spirit who filled Bezalel at the foot of Sinai as a figure of history, active once and long since withdrawn.

But the same Spirit still fills builders, and what they build still holds, because it rests on the one foundation that cannot be moved:

“For no one is able to lay another foundation besides the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:11).

You have been carrying one of those works in your pocket. Look closely, and you will find them everywhere.

Take up the tools of your age. Spend the gifts you were given. Build for the right kingdom.

Read the page for yourself. SQLite’s Code of Ethics sits on its official site at sqlite.org/codeofethics.html, all seventy-two lines, exactly where Hipp left it.
